name: Double-Head Rigging Sling, 3/4 in x 25 ft
title: Double-Head Rigging Sling 3/4 in x 25 ft
h1: Double-Head Rigging Sling, 3/4 in x 25 ft
meta: A 3/4 in x 25 ft double-head rigging sling for tying off big wood, choking stems and setting rigging points on removals. Typical price and buying notes.
tagline: A long, heavy rigging sling with an eye at each end for big removals and wide stems.
summary: This double-head rigging sling gives you 25 feet of 3/4 in rope with a spliced eye at each end, so you can wrap a wide trunk, choke a heavy leader or set a high rigging point without tying knots in your main line. It is built for crews that regularly bring down big wood.
highlights: Works as a choker, basket or girth hitch
Saves your rigging line from knots and wear

body.h: How crews use a long double-eye sling
p: On a removal, the sling usually goes around the stem above a crotch or a stout limb to set a block, or it gets choked around a piece you are about to cut so the rigging line has something clean to clip to. Twenty-five feet is long enough to go around trunks that a short sling simply will not reach, and you can still double it up on smaller wood.

Because both ends are spliced eyes, you can choke the sling through itself, pass one eye through the other, or clip both eyes into a block or carabiner for a basket. Pair it with a rigging block or ring and a dedicated rigging rope and you have the core of a lowering setup.
On the ground, a long sling also makes a solid anchor for a lowering device or a pull line when the base of the tree is too wide for a short strap.

body.h: Picking the right sling and keeping it in service
p: Size the sling to the load, not the other way around. Heavy pieces, shock loading and sharp bend angles all eat into working strength, so leave a generous margin and follow the manufacturer's rated loads and the ANSI Z133 standard. Only trained crew members should design rigging systems.

Inspect the sling before each job for cuts, glazing, melted fibers, pulled strands and wear at the splices. Retire it if you find damage you cannot explain. Keep it away from saw chain and bar oil, and let it dry before storing it in a rope bag.

faq.q: What does double-head mean on a rigging sling?
faq.a: It means the sling has an eye spliced into both ends, so you can choke it, basket it or clip both eyes into one connector without tying a knot.

faq.q: Can I use a rigging sling for climbing?
faq.a: No. Rigging slings are for moving wood, not for life support. Climbing anchors need gear rated and sold for that purpose, used by a trained climber.

name: Courant Cargo Bag 50L, Blue
title: Courant Bag: Cargo 50L Rope and Gear Bag, Blue
meta: This Courant bag, the Cargo 50L in blue, is a tough, open-top gear and rope bag for climbers who want saddle, lines and hardware in one place on the job.
tagline: A 50-liter carry bag that swallows a climbing line, saddle and hardware.
summary: The Courant bag known as the Cargo is a 50-liter carryall built for tree work, with room for a climbing line, a saddle and a pile of hardware in one load. The blue color makes it easy to spot in a truck bed or at the base of the tree.
highlights: Bright blue color is easy to find on site
Holds rope, saddle and hardware together

body.h: Why a dedicated gear bag helps
p: Life-support gear lasts longer and stays easier to inspect when it is not rattling around a truck box with saws, wedges and fuel. A bag like the Cargo keeps your climbing line, saddle and connectors together, off the ground and away from bar oil and two-stroke mix.
At 50 liters it handles a full climbing kit for a day of pruning or a removal. Many climbers keep one bag for the main line and saddle and a second smaller bag for throw line and spare hardware.
A bag with a wide mouth also makes the end of the day faster. Flake the rope straight in, drop the saddle on top and zip or cinch it, rather than coiling a line that will kink on the next job.

body.h: Living with it on the job
p: Pack the rope loosely so it feeds out without kinks, and set the bag where it will not get run over by the chipper or buried under brush. Let wet gear dry before it goes back in for the night.
A good bag does not replace inspection. Pull your gear out regularly, check it against the manufacturer's instructions, and retire anything that fails.
If you share a truck with other climbers, a distinct color like this blue makes it obvious whose kit is whose, which helps keep personal life-support gear with the person who inspects it.

faq.q: What fits in a 50L Courant Cargo bag?
faq.a: A typical climbing line of around 150 ft, a saddle, a few carabiners, a friction device and lanyard will usually fit, depending on rope diameter and how you pack it.

faq.q: Is the Cargo bag waterproof?
faq.a: Treat it as weather resistant rather than waterproof. Dry wet rope and saddles before storing them in any bag.

name: Replacement Rope Lanyard (No Snaps)
title: Replacement Rope Lanyard Without Snaps
meta: A replacement rope lanyard without snaps lets you rebuild a worn flipline with your own connectors and adjuster. What to look for, sizing and safety.
tagline: Rope-only lanyard for climbers rebuilding a worn flipline with their own hardware.
summary: A replacement rope lanyard without snaps is the rope section of a flipline sold on its own, so you can swap out a worn or damaged lanyard and keep using connectors and an adjuster you already trust. If you have cut, glazed or simply lost the rope part of your lanyard, this is the part you need.
highlights: Rope only, no snaps or carabiners included
Pairs with a mechanical adjuster or friction hitch
Cheaper than a complete new lanyard kit
Common lengths suit most spar and limb work
specs: Must meet ANSI Z133 as assembled

p: The flipline is the piece of gear that keeps you on the stem while you climb spurs on a removal or position yourself for a cut. It takes a beating: bark grit, saw near-misses, pitch and constant cycling through an adjuster. Most climbers wear out the rope long before the snaps and adjuster are done.

A replacement rope lanyard without snaps covers that situation. You keep your locking carabiners or snap and your adjuster, and replace only the rope. It is also a practical fix if the rope has gone missing from your kit or you want a second length for big trunks.

Pick a length that wraps the biggest wood you regularly climb with some tail left to manage. A shorter lanyard is easier to handle on small spars; a longer one gives you options on wide trunks and lets you double it up. Many climbers carry two: a standard flipline and a long one.

Check that the rope diameter matches your adjuster or hitch. A rope that is too thin or too thick for a mechanical adjuster can slip or jam. If you run a friction hitch instead, follow the hitch cord and rope combination the manufacturers recommend.

Some climbers like a lanyard with a spliced eye on one end and a knotted or stitched termination on the other, while others want eyes on both ends so they can choose how to clip it. Look at how your old lanyard was built and match it, or have a qualified person advise you before changing the design.

Because this is life-support equipment, the finished lanyard has to be assembled correctly with compatible, rated hardware. If you are not sure how to terminate the rope or which connectors are approved, have a qualified person do it or buy a complete lanyard. Life-support gear has to meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every use, and be used by trained climbers.

Never climb on a lanyard you cannot verify. Steel-core flipline is the usual choice when you are cutting close to the lanyard on removals; a rope lanyard without a core must be kept well clear of the saw. Pair the flipline with a second attachment when you cut, as Z133 requires two points of attachment for chainsaw work aloft.

Look at the full length before each climb. Retire it if you see cuts, melted or glazed sections, core showing through the cover, stiff spots or heavy contamination from fuel and bar oil. Keep the lanyard out of the sun when not in use and store it dry in a gear bag.
Write down when each new lanyard goes into service. Fliplines often get retired on condition alone, but knowing the age helps you spot one that has been in the kit too long.

faq.q: Does this lanyard come with snaps or carabiners?
faq.a: No. It is the rope only. You supply compatible, rated connectors and an adjuster, or have a qualified person assemble it.

faq.q: I lost the strap of my lanyard. Can I just replace the rope?
faq.a: Yes, if your hardware is still in good condition and inspected. Replace the rope section with one that matches your adjuster and connectors, and assemble it correctly before climbing.

faq.q: How often should a rope lanyard be replaced?
faq.a: There is no fixed date. Replace it whenever inspection turns up damage, contamination or heavy wear, and follow the manufacturer's service life guidance.

faq.q: Can I cut near a rope lanyard?
faq.a: Keep the saw well away from any rope lanyard. For close cutting on removals, many climbers prefer a steel-core flipline, plus a second point of attachment.

name: Sterling Shock Cord (By the Foot)
title: Sterling Shock Cord: Bungee Cord by the Foot
h1: Sterling Shock Cord, Bungee Cord by the Foot
meta: Sterling shock cord is bungee cord by the foot for gear loops, tool tethers, rope bag closures and truck tie-downs. Cut exactly the length you need.
tagline: Stretchy accessory cord cut to length for gear tethers, bag closures and tie-downs.
summary: Sterling shock cord is bungee cord by the foot, so you can cut exactly what you need for gear loops, tool keepers, bag closures and truck organization. It is a utility cord for the shop and the truck, not a life-support line.
highlights: Sold by the foot, cut to length
Elastic core with a braided cover
Handy for tool tethers and bag closures
Keeps the truck and trailer organized
Not for climbing or rigging loads

body.h: Where shock cord earns its keep
p: Most crews find a dozen uses for a few feet of bungee cord: a keeper on a handsaw scabbard, a closure on a throw-line cube, a stretch tether for a radio, or a quick tie-down to keep wedges and files from sliding around the truck box.
Buying it by the foot means you are not stuck with a pack of pre-made bungees with hooks that never fit. Tie your own ends, add cord locks or hog rings, and make exactly what the job needs.

On the climbing side, a short loop of shock cord on a saddle ring can keep a spare carabiner or a hand-saw lanyard tidy, as long as nothing load-bearing ever depends on it. In the shop, a few lengths keep coiled rigging lines and rolled-up tarps from coming undone between jobs.

Shock cord stretches by design and has a low strength compared with climbing or rigging rope. Never use it for life support, rigging loads or anything where a failure could drop a person or a piece of wood. Keep it to organization and light-duty tasks.
UV and heat break down the elastic over time. When the cord stops springing back or the cover starts to fray, cut a fresh piece.

faq.q: Can I use shock cord as a tool lanyard aloft?
faq.a: Only as a light tether for small items if it is rated for that use. For saws and heavier tools, use a lanyard made and rated for tools aloft.

faq.q: How do I finish the ends of shock cord?
faq.a: Most people tie a knot, use a hog ring or crimp, or add a cord lock. Seal the cut ends with heat to stop the cover from fraying.

name: Samson Arbor-Plex 1/2 in Rope
title: Samson Arbor-Plex 1/2 in 12-Strand Rope
meta: Samson Arbor Plex 1/2 in is a 12-strand single-braid line known for easy handling and simple splicing. How tree crews use it, sizing and typical price.
tagline: A 12-strand single-braid 1/2 in line with an easy hand and simple splicing.
summary: Samson Arbor Plex in 1/2 in is a 12-strand single-braid line that handles easily, runs well through blocks and is simple to splice. Tree crews mostly use it as a light rigging and utility line rather than a climbing rope.
highlights: Easy to splice eyes in the field
Light rigging, tag line and utility work

p: A 12-strand single braid has no separate cover and core, so it is quick to inspect and quick to splice. That makes 1/2 in Arbor-Plex a handy line for small-wood rigging, pulling limbs out of the way, tag lines and general work around the yard.
For lowering heavier wood, step up in size or use a double-braid rigging line such as the 3/4 in Arbor-Plex rigging rope.

Because it is light and flexible, it also makes a good line for a small speed line or for hauling tools aloft on a rope instead of a throw line, where the climber does not want to pull up a heavy rope.

Climbing lines need to be specifically rated and sold for life support and must suit your friction device or hitch. Check the manufacturer's documentation before using any line for climbing, and if it is not listed for that use, keep it on the rigging side. Life-support gear has to meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every use, and be used by trained climbers.
Inspect a single braid by looking along each strand for cuts, pulled or fused yarns and hard spots. Retire it if anything looks wrong.
Store it dry and out of the sun, and keep it in a bag separate from your climbing lines so nobody grabs the wrong rope in a hurry.

faq.q: Is Samson Arbor-Plex a climbing rope?
faq.a: It is generally sold and used as a rigging and utility line. Use only ropes the manufacturer rates for climbing as your life-support line.

faq.q: Is 12-strand rope easy to splice?
faq.a: Yes. Single-braid 12-strand is one of the easiest constructions to splice, which is a big part of its appeal for slings and eyes.

name: Teufelberger Safety Blue Climbing Rope (Blue/White)
title: Teufelberger Safety Blue Rope, 16-Strand Climbing Line
meta: Teufelberger Safety Blue is a classic blue rope for tree climbing: a 1/2 in 16-strand line with a firm cover that works with traditional friction hitches.
tagline: The classic blue-and-white 16-strand climbing line for traditional hitch climbers.
summary: Teufelberger Safety Blue is the blue rope a lot of climbers learned on: a 1/2 in 16-strand climbing line with a blue-and-white pattern that is easy to see in the canopy. It works well with traditional friction hitches and moving-rope techniques.
highlights: Blue and white pattern is easy to spot
Long track record in tree care
Good all-round line for DdRT climbing

body.h: Why climbers still reach for Safety Blue
p: A 16-strand line has a tight cover that holds its shape and resists picking up bark and debris. That firm hand works well with a Blake's hitch or Distel on a split tail, which is why this light blue rope has been a training and production line for a long time.
The blue-and-white color pattern is easy to follow through the crown, which helps the ground crew read where the climber is and keeps the line distinct from rigging rope.
It is a common first rope for new climbers learning moving-rope techniques, partly because so many trainers have climbed on it themselves and know how it behaves with the usual hitches.

Before you buy, check that your friction device, hitch cord and pulleys are approved for a 1/2 in line. Rope diameter and cover stiffness change how a hitch grabs, so test on the ground first. Life-support gear has to meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every use, and be used by trained climbers.
Keep it out of the sun when not in use, away from fuel and bar oil, and coiled loosely in a rope bag. Retire it when you see cover damage, core shots, glazing or stiff spots.

faq.q: What diameter is Teufelberger Safety Blue?
faq.a: It is a 1/2 in (about 12.7 mm) climbing line. Confirm compatibility with your hitch and hardware.

faq.q: Can I use Safety Blue for SRT?
faq.a: It is mostly used for moving-rope climbing. If you want it for SRT, check that your devices are approved for it and follow the manufacturers' instructions.

name: Teufelberger Ultra-Vee Climbing Rope
title: Ultra-Vee Teufelberger Rope for Tree Climbing
meta: Teufelberger rope Ultra-Vee is a 16-strand climbing line with a smooth, firm hand for hitch climbing on moving rope. Specs, fit, care and typical price.
tagline: A firm, smooth 16-strand climbing line for hitch climbers on moving rope.
summary: The Teufelberger rope called Ultra-Vee is a 16-strand climbing line with a smooth cover and a firm hand that holds up to daily hitch climbing. It suits climbers who want a predictable line for moving-rope work.
highlights: Holds its shape through daily use

p: Ultra-Vee is a fiber rope built for climbers who prefer a firm line. A firm cover keeps friction hitches consistent from the first climb to the hundredth, and it does not flatten out as quickly through a friction saver or a lanyard adjuster.
It runs well over a cambium saver or through a rigging ring and is easy to throw over a limb when you advance your line.

Climbers who already like Teufelberger fiber rope often pick Ultra-Vee for a production line because it keeps a consistent feel from new to well-used, which makes your hitch behave the same on Friday as it did on Monday.

Check that your hitch cord, friction device and pulleys are approved for the diameter. Try your setup low to the ground before climbing on a new line. Life-support gear has to meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every use, and be used by trained climbers.
Store it in a bag, out of the sun, away from fuel. Retire it if you find cover damage, core exposure, glazing or hard spots.
Rotate the ends now and then so wear is spread out, and keep notes on its age and use so you know when it is due for a closer look.

faq.q: Is Ultra-Vee good for beginners?
faq.a: It is a predictable line for moving-rope climbing, which makes it a reasonable choice for climbers in training, under supervision.

faq.q: What is the difference between 16-strand and 24-strand?
faq.a: 16-strand lines tend to be firmer with a coarser cover, while 24-strand lines are usually smoother and rounder. Both can be excellent; it comes down to your hitch and device.

name: Petzl Control 12.5 mm Climbing Rope
title: Petzl Climbing Rope: Control 12.5 mm Arborist Line
meta: The Petzl climbing rope called Control is a 12.5 mm arborist line built to pair with the Petzl ZigZag and other devices. Fit, handling, care and price.
tagline: A 12.5 mm arborist line made to run in Petzl mechanical friction devices.
summary: The Petzl Control is a 12.5 mm Petzl climbing rope made for tree work and designed to run in Petzl's mechanical devices such as the ZigZag. Climbers who buy Petzl ropes usually want that matched, predictable behavior.
highlights: Matched to Petzl mechanical friction devices
Good for both DdRT and SRT setups

p: Mechanical friction devices are sensitive to rope diameter and cover. A rope designed alongside the device gives you smoother descent and more predictable grab. That is the main reason climbers running a ZigZag or a similar device choose the Control.
It works on a moving-rope system or on a static line for SRT, depending on the devices and approvals in your kit.

Petzl ropes have a reputation for consistent diameter and cover, which matters with mechanical devices. A rope that swells or fuzzes up can change how much friction a device gives, so a stable line keeps your descent smooth from the first climb to the last.
The 24-strand-style cover is smoother than many 16-strand lines, which helps the rope feed through pulleys and devices without catching.

Read Petzl's instructions for the rope and every device you plan to use with it, and check compatibility before climbing. Life-support gear has to meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every use, and be used by trained climbers.
Keep it in a rope bag, away from sun, chemicals, fuel and bar oil. Retire it when inspection finds cover damage, core exposure, glazing or stiff sections.

faq.q: Will the Petzl Control work with non-Petzl devices?
faq.a: Possibly. Check the device manufacturer's list of compatible rope diameters and constructions before using it.

faq.q: Is 12.5 mm the same as 1/2 in?
faq.a: Close. 1/2 in is about 12.7 mm, so the two are similar, but device approvals are listed by diameter and construction, so check the specific rope.

name: Sterling 11 mm HTP Static Rope
title: Sterling HTP 11mm Static Rope for SRT
meta: Sterling HTP is an 11mm static rope with a tough polyester build for SRT access lines and rescue kits. Handling, compatibility, care and typical price.
tagline: A tough, low-stretch 11 mm polyester static line for SRT and rescue kits.
summary: Sterling HTP is an 11mm static rope with a polyester build that stretches very little, which makes it a solid choice for SRT access lines and rescue kits. Its firm, abrasion-resistant sheath stands up to bark and edges.
highlights: Good for SRT access and rescue kits
Compact and light compared with 1/2 in lines

body.h: Where an 11mm rope fits in tree work
p: A thinner static line is lighter to carry up and easier to install for SRT, especially on tall trees where rope weight adds up. Low stretch means less bounce when you ascend, so more of your effort goes into gaining height.
Many climbers also keep an 11 mm static line in a rescue or access kit because it packs small and handles edges well.
An 11mm rope also takes up less space in the rope bag, which matters if you carry a separate line for access, for a second climber or for a rescue setup.

Not every arborist friction device or hitch is approved for 11 mm rope. Check the approved diameter range for your descender, ascenders and hitch cord before you buy. Life-support gear has to meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every use, and be used by trained climbers.
Keep it clean and dry, out of UV when stored, and retire it when the sheath is damaged, the core shows, or it develops stiff or glazed spots.
Thinner ropes can give less friction in some devices, so expect to adjust your setup and practice descents close to the ground first.

faq.q: Is an 11mm rope thick enough for tree climbing?
faq.a: It can be, as long as every device and hitch in your system is approved for 11 mm. Many arborist devices are sized for 11 to 13 mm, but check each one.

faq.q: Why choose static over dynamic rope?
faq.a: Static rope stretches very little, which makes ascending and working on a fixed line more efficient. Dynamic rope is for lead climbing falls, which is not how tree climbers normally work.

name: Sterling WorkPro 12.5 mm Static Rope
title: Sterling WorkPro 12.5mm Static Climbing Rope
meta: Sterling WorkPro 12.5mm is a static climbing rope sized for the arborist devices most climbers run. Handling, SRT use, care and typical price.
tagline: A 12.5 mm static line sized for the friction devices most arborists use.
summary: Sterling WorkPro 12.5mm is a static climbing rope made in the diameter that most arborist friction devices and hitches are designed around. It is a straightforward choice for SRT climbers who want low stretch and a durable sheath.
highlights: 12.5 mm diameter suits most arborist devices
Durable sheath for bark and edges
Works for SRT and rope access

p: Most mechanical devices and many hitch cords are designed with 11.5 to 13 mm rope in mind, and 12.5 mm sits right in that range. That gives you more options when you build or upgrade your SRT kit.
The static build keeps bounce to a minimum on long ascents, and the heavier sheath stands up to repeated base anchors and redirects.

If you are moving from a 1/2 in moving-rope line into SRT, a 12.5 mm static line keeps the same feel in your hand while giving you the low stretch that makes rope walking efficient. It is also a sensible size for a base-anchored SRT line that will be redirected through several unions.
Sterling builds the sheath to take abuse, which helps when the rope runs over rough bark or sits in a basal anchor all day.

Confirm every device in your system lists 12.5 mm as approved. Life-support gear has to meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every use, and be used by trained climbers.
Store it in a rope bag, dry and out of the sun. Retire it if you find cuts, core exposure, glazing or stiff sections.
Write the date it went into service on a tag or in a log, so you can track age and use along with what you see during inspection.

faq.q: Can I use WorkPro for moving-rope climbing?
faq.a: It can work on a moving-rope system if your hitch or device is approved for it, but static lines are most often used for SRT.

faq.q: How long should my climbing rope be?
faq.a: Most climbers want a line at least twice the height of their typical tie-in point for DdRT, plus a margin. For SRT, the rope needs to reach the ground from your anchor with tail to spare.

name: Samson 1/2 in Rigging Rope
title: Samson 1/2 in Rigging Rope for Tree Work
meta: Samson 1/2 in rigging rope for lowering small and medium wood, pulling limbs and tag lines. How to pick a size, what it handles and how to care for it.
tagline: A 1/2 in rigging line for small-to-medium wood, pull lines and everyday lowering.
summary: This Samson 1/2 in rigging rope is the everyday line for lowering small and medium wood, pulling tops over and running tag lines on pruning and removal jobs. It is light enough to carry up and throw around, yet built for the abuse rigging lines take.
highlights: Light enough to haul aloft and throw
Runs through blocks, rings and bollards
Good for pull lines and tag lines
From a long-standing arborist rope maker
specs: Light-to-medium wood, pull and tag lines

body.h: Where a 1/2 in rigging line fits
p: Most crews carry rigging rope in at least two sizes. The 1/2 in line is the one that gets used every day: lowering limbs over a roof, snubbing small tops, guiding brush away from a fence or pulling a tree in the felling direction. It is easy to manage on a crowded job site and fast to flake out.
For big wood, step up to a 5/8 in or 3/4 in line like the Samson 3/4 in Arbor-Plex. Keeping a lighter line for lighter work spares the big rope from wear and keeps your groundie's arms fresh.

Samson arborist rope has been part of tree crews' kits for a long time, and a Samson line in 1/2 in is one of the most common rigging ropes on residential jobs. Samson cordage is also widely available, which makes replacing a worn line straightforward.

Look at the heaviest piece you plan to lower, the drop distance and whether you will be letting it run or stopping it short. Shock loading multiplies forces quickly, so working loads are a fraction of breaking strength. Follow Samson's rated values and the ANSI Z133 standard, and leave a wide margin.
Construction matters too. Double-braid lines are strong and handle well in blocks and lowering devices. Single-braid lines are easier to splice and inspect. Many crews end up with both.

Also think about the hardware. A 1/2 in rope needs blocks, pulleys and lowering devices sized for it. A rope that is too small for a sheave can wear quickly or slip, and one that is too large can jam.

Set the block on sound wood, keep the rope clean of the cut, and use a lowering device or a friction wrap around the trunk so the groundie controls the load. Communicate before every cut. A trained crew member should plan the rigging, especially when anything near a structure or line is involved.
Keep the rope out of the chipper infeed and away from chain and bar oil. Flake it into a bag at the end of the day rather than coiling it tight.
Tag lines are a good use for an older 1/2 in rope that is still sound but no longer trusted for lowering.

Run the rope through your hands before each job. Look for cuts, glazing from friction, flattened or hard spots, pulled strands and core showing through the cover. A rigging line that has caught a big shock load should be looked at carefully. Retire it when in doubt, and never use a rigging line for climbing.

Keep a simple log for each rigging line: when it went into service, any heavy shock loads, and notes from inspections. Mark lines by size and purpose so a climbing line never gets used for rigging or the other way round.

faq.q: What is the best rope for rigging trees?
faq.a: There is no single best. A 1/2 in line covers most light rigging, while big wood calls for 5/8 in or 3/4 in. Match rope size and construction to the load and your hardware.

faq.q: How much weight can 1/2 in rigging rope hold?
faq.a: Check the manufacturer's rated breaking strength and apply a generous safety factor. Dynamic loads from a falling piece can be many times the static weight.

faq.q: Can I climb on rigging rope?
faq.a: No. Use only ropes rated and sold for climbing as life-support lines.

faq.q: How long should a rigging line be?
faq.a: Long enough to reach from the block to the ground, wrap a friction device or trunk and leave the groundie working room. 150 ft and 200 ft are common.

name: Samson Arbor-Plex 3/4 in Rigging Rope
title: Samson Rope Arbor-Plex 3/4 in Rigging Rope
h1: Samson Rope Arbor-Plex 3/4 in Rigging Rope
meta: Samson rope Arbor-Plex in 3/4 in is a 12-strand rigging line for heavy wood, easy to splice and inspect. Sizing, use on removals, care and typical price.
tagline: A 3/4 in 12-strand rigging line for heavy wood on big removals.
summary: Samson rope Arbor-Plex in 3/4 in is a 12-strand single-braid rigging line built for lowering heavy wood on big removals. It is easy to splice and easy to inspect, which matters on a line that takes serious loads every day.
highlights: Easy to inspect strand by strand
Runs well through big blocks and lowering devices
Made by Samson, a long-time arborist rope maker

body.h: What the 3/4 in Arbor-Plex is for
p: When the pieces get big, the rope has to step up. A 3/4 in line is what crews run on removals where they are blocking down heavy trunk sections, lowering wide leaders or speed-lining big wood over obstacles. It gives you the strength margin those loads demand.
Pair it with a block and sling sized to match, such as a 3/4 in double-head rigging sling, and a lowering device anchored at the base.

Most crews do not need a 3/4 in rigging rope every day. It comes out for large removals, crane-assist jobs where pieces still need control, and situations where a smaller rope simply would not give enough margin. Having it on the truck means you are not tempted to push a lighter line past what it should handle.

A 12-strand single braid has no separate cover, so what you see is the load-bearing structure. That makes inspection straightforward and splicing quick, whether you need a spliced eye for a sling or want to repair the end of a line. Many climbers who search for sampson rope or Samson line are looking for exactly this kind of easy-to-work rigging line.
The trade-off is that a single braid can pick up more abrasion than a covered rope, so keep it off sharp edges and rough bark where you can.
Splicing your own eyes also lets you make up custom-length slings from the same rope, so the whole system matches.

Heavy rigging puts big forces on the rope, block, sling and the tree itself. Plan the system before the first cut, consider shock loading, and use the manufacturer's rated values and ANSI Z133 to stay well inside working limits. Only trained, experienced crew members should set up heavy rigging.
Keep everyone clear of the drop zone and the rope's path, and agree on clear calls between climber and ground before every piece.

Make sure every piece of hardware in the system is rated for the same loads as the rope: block, sling, lowering device and connectors. A strong rope does not help if the block or sling is the weak link.

Inspect each strand for cuts, pulled yarns, fused or glazed sections from friction, and stiff spots. A rope that has taken a severe shock load deserves extra scrutiny. Keep it out of fuel, bar oil and sunlight in storage, and retire it rather than gamble on a damaged line.
A 3/4 in line is heavy, especially when wet. Flake it into a large bag rather than coiling it, and use a rope bag with good handles so the groundie is not dragging it through the dirt between jobs.
Mark each end with tape or a label showing size and date in service, so the crew can tell it apart from lighter rigging lines at a glance.

faq.q: Is Samson rope the same as Sampson rope?
faq.a: Yes. Sampson is a common misspelling. The company is Samson Rope.

faq.q: What is Arbor-Plex made of?
faq.a: It is a 12-strand single braid made from a synthetic fiber blend. Check Samson's current product sheet for the exact fiber and strength figures.

faq.q: Is 3/4 in rope too heavy for everyday rigging?
faq.a: For light pruning it is more than you need. Most crews carry a lighter 1/2 in line for everyday work and save the 3/4 in for big wood.

faq.q: Can Arbor-Plex be spliced?
faq.a: Yes. 12-strand single braid is one of the easier ropes to splice, which is a big reason crews choose it.

name: Samson Stable Braid 5/8 in Rigging Rope
title: Samson Stable Braid 5/8 Rope for Rigging
h1: Samson Stable Braid 5/8 Rope for Rigging
meta: Samson Stable Braid is a 5/8 rope with a double-braid polyester build for medium-to-heavy rigging. Lengths including 200 ft, care tips and typical price.
tagline: A 5/8 in double-braid rigging line for medium-to-heavy wood.
summary: Samson Stable Braid is a 5/8 rope with a double-braid polyester construction, a workhorse middle size for rigging medium and heavy wood. It holds its shape well and runs smoothly through blocks and lowering devices.
highlights: Steps up from 1/2 in for bigger wood

body.h: The middle size most crews need
p: A 5/8 in line handles the pieces that are too big for a 1/2 in rope but do not justify hauling out the 3/4 in. It is a good default for removals on residential lots where you are lowering leaders and trunk sections of moderate size.
A 200 ft of rope length gives plenty of reach from a high block to a lowering device at the base, with tail for the groundie.

Samson Stable Braid has a firm, round build that keeps its shape on a capstan or bollard, so the groundie gets predictable friction when letting a piece run. Crews often pair a 5/8 rope with a matching block and sling for medium removals.
Plan the rigging, account for shock loading, and stay within the manufacturer's rated values and ANSI Z133. A trained crew member should set up every rigging system.
Inspect the cover and feel for flat or stiff spots before each use. Keep it out of fuel and bar oil, flake it into a bag, and retire it if it is damaged. Never use rigging rope for climbing.
Rotate which end you use for the block so wear does not concentrate in one spot, and spliced eyes should be checked closely since they take a lot of the load.

faq.q: Is 5/8 rope good for tree rigging?
faq.a: Yes. It is a common middle size that handles medium-to-heavy wood. Match it to the load and your block and sling.

faq.q: How long is a typical Stable Braid rigging line?
faq.a: 200 ft is popular for rigging because it reaches from a high block to the ground with room to spare. Check the listing for available lengths.

name: All Gear Heavy Duty Chafe Sleeve
title: All Gear Heavy Duty Chafe Sleeve: Rope Chafe Gear
h1: All Gear Heavy Duty Chafe Sleeve (Rope Chafe Gear)
meta: The All Gear heavy duty chafe sleeve is chafe gear that slides over rope and slings to shield them from rough bark, crotches and edges. Uses and care.
tagline: A tough sleeve that protects rope and slings from bark, crotches and edges.
summary: The All Gear heavy duty chafe sleeve is chafe gear that slides over a rope or sling to protect it where it bears on rough bark, a tight crotch or a hard edge. It adds life to rigging lines and slings that take abrasion every day.

p: Any spot where rope or a sling rubs on bark, concrete or a sharp edge wears out fast. Slip a sleeve over that section, such as a sling choked around a rough stem, a rope running over a building edge or a rigging line bearing on a crotch, and the sleeve takes the wear instead.
It is a cheap way to make a big rope purchase last longer.

The heavy-duty build is aimed at rigging, where slings and lines see far more abrasion than a climbing line does. Use it where a sling is choked around rough bark for a block, or where a lowering line runs over a crotch on its way to the ground.
Climbers sometimes add one to a basal anchor so the rope is not grinding on the trunk while they work above.
A sleeve slows abrasion; it does not make a damaged rope safe. Keep inspecting the rope under the sleeve, and retire anything that shows damage. A sleeve also will not stop a saw.
Check the sleeve for holes and worn-through spots and replace it when it stops covering the rope fully.
Thread it on before you build the system. Trying to add a sleeve to a loaded rope is awkward and can be unsafe.

faq.q: What is chafe gear for rope?
faq.a: Chafe gear is any sleeve or wrap that protects rope from abrasion where it rubs on bark, edges or hardware.

faq.q: Can I use a chafe sleeve on a climbing line?
faq.a: Yes, many climbers use sleeves at edges or on a basal anchor. It protects the rope but does not replace inspection.

name: Chafe Sleeve
title: Rope Chafe Sleeve for Rigging and Climbing Lines
meta: A simple rope chafe sleeve that slides over rigging lines and slings to protect against chaffing at crotches, bark and edges. How to use it and care for it.
tagline: A basic slide-on sleeve that keeps rope and slings from chafing.
summary: A chafe sleeve is a simple tube of tough fabric that slides over a rope or sling to stop chafing where it rubs on bark, crotches or edges. It is an inexpensive way to protect lines that cost a lot more to replace.
highlights: Slides on over rope or sling
Useful for rigging and basal anchors

body.h: Simple protection that pays for itself
p: Rope rarely wears evenly. One spot over a crotch or around a rough trunk takes most of the damage. Sliding a chafe sleeve over that spot spreads the wear onto a cheap, replaceable part.

Crews use them on slings choked around rough bark, on basal anchors, and anywhere a rope runs over a hard edge. If you want a thicker build for heavy rigging, look at the All Gear heavy duty chafe sleeve.
Sleeves are light enough to clip a couple to your saddle or keep in the rigging bag, so they are on hand when you spot a rubbing point mid-job.
A sleeve is protection, not a repair. Still inspect the rope under it, and retire damaged lines. Replace the sleeve when it is worn through.
Store it with the rope it protects so it is there when you need it.
Thread the sleeve on before you load the rope. Moving a sleeve on a loaded line is awkward and can leave the rope exposed right where it needs protecting.
Wash a dirty sleeve the same way you would clean rope, since grit trapped inside can wear the line it is meant to protect.

faq.q: What is chaffing gear?
faq.a: Chaffing gear, or chafe gear, is any sleeve or wrap that protects a rope from abrasion at rub points.

faq.q: Does a chafe sleeve reduce rope strength?
faq.a: No. It sits over the rope and does not change its strength. It only protects the surface from wear.

name: Teufelberger Epicord 8 mm Hitch Cord (By the Foot)
title: Teufelberger Epicord 8mm Hitch Cord by the Foot
meta: Teufelberger Epicord is an 8mm hitch cord sold by the foot for friction hitches and split tails. Cut your own length, fit it to your rope and climb.
tagline: An 8 mm hitch cord by the foot for building friction hitches and split tails.
summary: Teufelberger Epicord is an 8 mm hitch cord sold by the foot, so you can cut exactly the length you need for your friction hitch, split tail or prusik loop. Climbers like it for a consistent grab and a cover that handles heat from descending.
highlights: Cut to length for your hitch style
Pairs well with common 11 to 13 mm climbing lines

p: Hitch cord length depends on the hitch you tie, the diameter of your climbing line and how you terminate the ends. A Distel, VT or Michoacán each wants a different length. Buying by the foot lets you get it right instead of making do with a pre-sewn cord.
Tie and test any new hitch low to the ground. If it grabs too hard or slips, adjust wraps or length before you climb.

Epicord is a popular hitch cord because it grabs consistently and holds up to the heat a hitch builds on long descents. Many climbers keep a few feet extra in the truck so they can tie a fresh hitch when the old one glazes.

Cord ends must be terminated correctly, either with appropriate stopper knots tied and dressed properly or with sewn eyes from a qualified source. If you are not sure, buy a pre-made eye-to-eye. Life-support gear has to meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every use, and be used by trained climbers.
Hitch cords wear faster than rope. Retire one at the first sign of glazing, stiffness or cover damage.
Keep spare cord dry and out of the sun until you need it, and label it so it does not get mixed up with utility cord.

faq.q: How long should my Epicord hitch be?
faq.a: It depends on the hitch and your rope. Many climbers cut around 28 to 32 inches for a typical Distel with knotted ends, but test and adjust for your setup.

faq.q: Will 8 mm Epicord work on my climbing line?
faq.a: It is commonly used on 11 to 13 mm lines. Check the manufacturer's guidance for compatibility with your rope.

name: Yale Cordage R.I.N.G. Rope (By the Foot)
title: Yale Cordage R.I.N.G. Rope, Sold by the Foot
h1: Yale Cordage R.I.N.G. Rope by the Foot
meta: Yale Cordage R.I.N.G. rope is technical cord sold by the foot for custom loops, eye-to-eyes and rigging pieces. Who it suits, how to use it, typical price.
tagline: Technical cord by the foot for climbers who build their own loops and rigging pieces.
summary: Yale Cordage R.I.N.G. rope is a technical cord sold by the foot, so climbers and riggers can build custom loops, eye-to-eyes and small rigging components to the exact length they want. Yale rope has a strong following in tree care for consistent construction and good splicing behavior.
highlights: Sold by the foot, cut to your length
From Yale Cordage, a US rope maker
For custom loops and small rigging pieces
Lets you match length to your setup
Avoids paying for pre-made lengths you do not need

body.h: Why buy cordage by the foot
p: Pre-made slings and eye-to-eyes come in fixed lengths that rarely match exactly what you want. If you run a particular hitch, a specific rigging setup or a custom friction saver, buying Yale cordage by the foot lets you build pieces that fit your kit and your climbing style.
It also makes sense for crews that make up their own short slings, loopies and retrieval loops in the shop, where a few extra feet on the spool keeps work moving when something wears out.
Ordering by the foot also keeps waste down. Instead of buying a full hank to make two short loops, you buy what the project needs, plus a little extra for practice splices and trimming.

body.h: What R.I.N.G. rope is used for
p: Most climbers who order this cord use it for small, purpose-built components: loops that go around a limb, short eye-to-eye pieces, or retrieval and utility lines on the rigging side. The exact diameter and strength depend on the version you order, so check the listing and Yale's product information before you plan a build.
If you are after a hitch cord rather than a utility loop, look at a dedicated hitch cord like Teufelberger Epicord, which is made for friction hitches.

Yale rope technologies are known in tree care for precise braiding, which helps splices come out consistent. Crews that already like Yale ropes for climbing and rigging often stick with the same maker for their custom cordage so everything handles alike.

Anything that will hold a climber has to be built correctly. Splices and terminations on life-support components should be made by a qualified splicer following the rope maker's procedures, and many crews prefer to buy those pieces finished. Tying knots in cord reduces its strength, so account for that in any system. Life-support gear has to meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every use, and be used by trained climbers.
For rigging pieces, stay inside the manufacturer's rated values and follow ANSI Z133. Shock loads in rigging can be far higher than the weight of the wood.

Store spare cord dry, out of the sun and away from fuel and bar oil. Once it is in service, check it before each use for glazing, cuts, pulled strands and stiff spots, and retire any piece that is worn or that has taken a hard shock load.
Label each finished piece with its length and the date it went into service. Small cordage parts are easy to lose track of, and a log makes inspection and retirement easier.
Keep finished components separate from bulk cord so nobody grabs an untested length off the spool and puts it into a system.

faq.q: Is Yale cordage the same as Yale rope?
faq.a: Yes. Yale Cordage is the company; people often just call its products Yale rope.

faq.q: Can I splice R.I.N.G. rope myself?
faq.a: If you are trained and follow Yale's splicing instructions. For life-support components, many climbers have a qualified splicer do it or buy pre-made pieces.

faq.q: What diameter is the R.I.N.G. rope?
faq.a: Check the product listing for the version you order. Diameter and strength vary by version, and both determine what the cord can be used for.

faq.q: How much cord should I order?
faq.a: Plan the finished length of each piece, add enough for splices or knots, and add a little extra for trimming. When in doubt, order a few feet more.

name: Tree Access SRT Chest Harness
title: Tree Access SRT Climbing Chest Harness
h1: Tree Access SRT Climbing Chest Harness
meta: The Tree Access SRT chest harness is a climbing chest harness that holds a chest ascender or rope runner close for efficient SRT ascents. Fit and use.
tagline: A simple chest harness that keeps your SRT ascent system tight and efficient.
summary: The Tree Access SRT chest harness is a climbing chest harness that holds a chest ascender or the top of your rope-walking system close to your body, so every step on an SRT ascent turns into height. It adds very little weight to your saddle.
highlights: Holds a chest ascender or rope runner close
Also helps with gear organization on the chest

body.h: Why a chest harness for SRT
p: On a single-rope ascent, the chest ascender needs to stay high and tight so the rope feeds through as you step up. A chest harness holds it in place instead of letting it flop forward, which saves effort on long ascents.
It also helps keep your rope-walking system aligned so the foot and knee ascenders work smoothly.

A chest harness also gives you a handy place to carry a small light, a radio or a phone where you can reach it without digging into your saddle pockets, as long as nothing interferes with your ascent system.
Climbers moving into SRT often find the chest harness is the piece that makes their system feel smooth instead of awkward.

Adjust it snug but comfortable, and check that it works with your saddle and devices according to each manufacturer's instructions. A chest harness is usually not a life-support attachment on its own, so never use it as your primary tie-in unless the manufacturer says it is rated for that. Life-support gear has to meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every use, and be used by trained climbers.
Inspect webbing and buckles for cuts, fraying and damage before each climb.
Try it on with your saddle and full ascent kit on the ground before you climb, and adjust it so it does not pull you forward or ride up when you sit back.

faq.q: Is a chest harness required for SRT?
faq.a: Not always, but most rope-walking systems work better with one because it keeps the chest ascender tight to the rope.

faq.q: Can I hang from the chest harness?
faq.a: Only if the manufacturer rates it for that. Most SRT chest harnesses are positioning aids, not life-support attachments.

name: ISC Nessie Lanyard Management Clip
title: ISC Nessie Lanyard Management Clip
meta: The ISC Nessie is a lanyard management clip that keeps your flipline tidy on the saddle when you are not using it. How it works and who it suits.
tagline: A small saddle clip that keeps a flipline stowed and out of the way.
summary: The ISC Nessie is a lanyard management clip that holds your flipline neatly on the saddle when you are not using it, so the tail does not dangle and snag on limbs. It is a small piece of kit that makes moving through the canopy cleaner.
highlights: Keeps lanyard stowed on the saddle
Stops the tail snagging on limbs
Quick to clip in and out

p: A flipline hanging loose from your saddle catches on stubs, gets in the way of the saw and drags through the dirt between climbs. The Nessie gives the lanyard a home on your saddle so it stays organized until you need it.
Climbers who work removals with spikes and a flipline all day tend to appreciate it most.

Keeping the lanyard stowed also protects it. A tail dragging on the ground picks up grit, and a loose flipline near the saw is a hazard. A stowed lanyard is cleaner, safer and ready to throw when you reach the next limb.

The Nessie is a storage clip, not a life-support connector. Never clip into it as an anchor or attachment point. Life-support gear has to meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every use, and be used by trained climbers.
Check it for cracks and wear along with the rest of your saddle gear.
Mount it where you can reach it with either hand and where it does not interfere with your bridge, tie-in or other attachment points.
If it cracks, bends or stops holding the lanyard securely, replace it. It is a cheap part.

faq.q: Is the ISC Nessie a load-rated carabiner?
faq.a: No. It is a gear management clip for stowing a lanyard, not a life-support connector.

faq.q: Where does the Nessie mount?
faq.a: On your saddle, where it can hold the lanyard out of the way. Follow ISC's instructions for placement.

name: Rock Exotica Transporter XL
title: Rock Exotica Transporter XL Gear Carrier
meta: The Rock Exotica Transporter XL is a big-capacity gear carrier that clips to your saddle to hold hardware, slings and tools. Uses, fit and typical price.
tagline: A large gear carrier that holds hardware and slings on your saddle.
summary: The Rock Exotica Transporter XL is a large gear carrier that hangs from your saddle and holds a pile of carabiners, slings, pulleys and small tools where you can reach them. The XL size suits climbers who carry a lot of rigging hardware aloft.
highlights: Large capacity for hardware and slings
Clips to saddle gear loops or rings

p: On a rigging-heavy removal, a climber can be carrying several blocks, slings and connectors. Clipping them all to saddle loops gets messy fast. A dedicated carrier like the Transporter XL keeps that hardware together and easy to grab one-handed.
Many climbers hang one on each side: rigging gear on one, climbing spares on the other.
It also helps on the ground. Load it up with the slings and carabiners for the next rigging point and send it up on a tool line, so the climber can clip the whole set to the saddle at once.

A gear carrier is for storage only. Never use it as an anchor, tie-in or connector in a life-support or rigging system. Life-support gear has to meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every use, and be used by trained climbers.
Check it for cracks, deformation and sharp edges that could damage slings.
Hang it where it does not swing into your work, interfere with your lanyard or crowd your tie-in. Keep the heavy pieces toward the back so they do not pull the saddle off center.
Clear it before you descend so nothing is left hanging that could drop on the ground crew.

faq.q: Can I clip into the Transporter XL?
faq.a: No. It is a gear carrier, not a load-rated connector.

faq.q: What is the difference between the Transporter and the XL?
faq.a: The XL is the larger size, with more room for hardware and slings.

name: Chainsaw Protective Chaps and Pants
title: Chainsaw Safety Gear: Protective Chaps and Pants
h1: Chainsaw Safety Gear: Chaps and Protective Pants
meta: Chainsaw safety gear for tree work: how protective chaps and chainsaw protective pants work, what to look for, fit, care and when to replace them.
tagline: Leg protection for anyone who runs a saw, from occasional bucking to daily climbing.
summary: Chainsaw safety gear starts with leg protection, because legs take most saw injuries on the ground. Chainsaw protective clothing like chaps and saw pants uses layers of long fibers that pull out and jam the sprocket when a moving chain hits them, which can stop the chain before it reaches you.
highlights: Leg protection is the core of chainsaw safety gear
Chaps strap over your work pants
Saw pants build protection into the garment
Fibers jam the drive sprocket on contact
Look for labels showing the standard met
Replace after any cut that reaches the inner layers
specs: Front of legs, groin to ankle
Check the label for the standard met
Chaps: straps and buckles; pants: built in

p: Chainsaw chaps and saw pants contain several layers of long synthetic fibers under the outer shell. When a moving chain cuts the shell, it drags those fibers out and wraps them into the drive sprocket, which stops or slows the chain in a fraction of a second. That is why a cut chap must be retired: the protective layers have done their job once.
No leg protection makes you saw-proof. It reduces the chance and severity of an injury when something goes wrong. Good technique, a sharp chain, working chain brake and a clear work area come first.

Most chainsaw safety clothing protects the front of the legs, where contact is most likely. Some pants add protection around the calves as well. Check the coverage area on the label so you know what is protected.

Chaps are a wrap that buckles over your regular work pants. They are quick to put on, easy to share sizes across a crew, and the cheapest way to get protection. On hot days some people find them easier to vent.

Chainsaw safety pants build the protective layers into the trousers. They move with you, do not snag as easily and are the usual choice for climbers and full-time ground crew who run a saw all day. They cost more but tend to get worn more consistently, which matters more than anything.

Climbers have their own considerations. Some climbing saw pants are designed to be lighter and more breathable for work aloft, and some climbers wear them every day for consistency. Pick what you will actually wear on hot days and long climbs.

body.h: Fit, standards and the rest of the kit
p: Pick a length that covers from the waist to about 2 in below the top of your boot, without bunching. Check the label for the standard the gear meets and follow the manufacturer's instructions. In the US, ANSI Z133 calls for leg protection when operating a chainsaw on the ground. Requirements for climbers working aloft differ, so check the current standard and your employer's policy.
Leg protection is one part of a full kit: a helmet with a visor or safety glasses, hearing protection, gloves and solid boots. Gear only helps if it is worn every time the saw is running.

Wash protective clothing according to the label, since dirt and oil can reduce how well the fibers pull free. Inspect before use and retire any chaps or pants where a cut has reached the protective layers, or where the outer shell is badly worn or torn. Do not patch them with anything that could stop the fibers from pulling out.
Keep a spare set on the truck so a cut pair can be replaced on the spot instead of someone working unprotected until the next order arrives.

faq.q: What is the most important chainsaw safety gear?
faq.a: Leg protection, eye and hearing protection, a helmet, gloves and proper boots. Most ground saw injuries involve the legs, so chaps or saw pants are essential.

faq.q: Are chainsaw chaps or chainsaw safety pants better?
faq.a: Both protect when they meet the relevant standard. Pants are more comfortable for all-day use; chaps are cheaper and quick to put on.

faq.q: Can I wash chainsaw chaps?
faq.a: Yes, following the manufacturer's label. Avoid harsh treatments the label warns against.

faq.q: When should I replace chainsaw protective pants?
faq.a: After any cut that reaches the inner protective layers, or when the shell is worn through or the label says to retire them.

name: 3M Peltor LiteCom FRS Headset
title: 3M Peltor LiteCom FRS Two-Way Radio Headset
meta: The 3M Peltor LiteCom FRS is a hearing protection headset with a built-in two-way radio, so climber and ground crew can talk over the saw and chipper.
tagline: Hearing protection with a built-in FRS radio for climber-to-ground talk.
summary: The 3M Peltor LiteCom FRS is a hearing protection headset with a built-in two-way radio, so a climber and the ground crew can talk clearly over saws and the chipper. LiteCom headsets are a common upgrade for crews tired of shouting and hand signals.
highlights: Hearing protection and radio in one
Keeps calls clear over saw noise

p: Rigging calls, drop-zone clears and tie-in changes all depend on the climber and ground crew understanding each other. A radio headset makes those calls clear, hands-free and quick, which cuts confusion and speeds up the job.
Because the radio is built into the hearing protection, you are not trading safety for communication.
The LiteCom also lets the ground crew warn the climber about a hazard they cannot see, like someone walking into the drop zone or a vehicle approaching, without waiting for the saw to stop.

Check that the headset fits over or with your helmet; many crews use a helmet-mount version. Make sure the whole crew is on compatible radios and the same channel before the first cut. Follow 3M's instructions for fit, battery care and radio use.
Radio is a supplement, not a replacement for agreed hand signals and a clear call-and-response system. Keep backup signals ready in case a battery dies.
Hearing protection only works if the seal is good. Check the cushions for cracks and replace them when they get hard, and keep hair and glasses arms from breaking the seal.
Charge or swap batteries at the end of each day so the headset is ready for the next morning.

faq.q: Can LiteCom headsets talk to other FRS radios?
faq.a: FRS radios on the same channel can generally communicate. Check 3M's documentation and test with your crew's radios.

faq.q: Does the LiteCom work with a helmet?
faq.a: Helmet-mount versions are available. Check the model and your helmet's compatibility before ordering.

name: Sena 33i Bluetooth Communication System with Mesh Intercom
title: Sena 33i Bluetooth Intercom with Mesh
meta: The Sena 33i is a Bluetooth intercom with Mesh that lets climbers and ground crew talk hands-free on the job. Setup, helmet fit and typical price.
tagline: A Bluetooth intercom with Mesh for hands-free climber and ground crew talk.
summary: The Sena 33i is a Bluetooth intercom system with Mesh intercom that lets a climber and ground crew talk hands-free without carrying separate radios. Crews like Sena bluetooth intercom systems for quick pairing and clear audio.

p: Mount the unit on each crew member's helmet, connect over Mesh, and everyone can talk without pushing a button. That makes rigging calls, drop-zone clears and climber requests faster and clearer.
The 33i was designed for riders, so check fit on your helmet and how it works alongside your hearing protection.

Mesh intercom lets several people join the same conversation, so the climber, the groundie on the lowering device and the person running the chipper can all hear the same calls. That cuts down on relayed messages and missed warnings.
Bluetooth also lets you take a phone call or check directions between jobs without taking the helmet off.
Keep it charged and protected from sawdust and rain as well as you can. Range and audio depend on terrain and setup, so test on site.
Radio talk does not replace agreed hand signals and a clear call-and-response routine. Have a backup plan if a unit dies.
Make sure the speakers do not interfere with your hearing protection. Communication gear should never replace earmuffs or plugs around saws and chippers.
Follow your helmet maker's guidance on accessories, and do not drill or modify a helmet shell to mount it.

faq.q: Is the Sena 33i made for arborists?
faq.a: It is a general-purpose Bluetooth intercom, often used by riders. Many crews adapt it for tree work, but check helmet fit and hearing protection.

faq.q: Do all crew members need a Sena 33i?
faq.a: Each person needs a compatible Mesh-capable Sena unit to join the intercom.

name: Sena Integrated Communication Helmet System
title: Sena Communication System for Work Helmets
meta: A Sena communication system built into a work helmet setup, for arborist crews who want hands-free talk between climber and ground. Fit, use and price.
tagline: Helmet-integrated communication for crews who want hands-free talk.
summary: This Sena communication system integrates the headset into a helmet setup, giving arborist crews hands-free talk between the climber and ground without loose radios or clip-on parts. It suits crews that want communication built in rather than added on.
highlights: Communication built into the helmet setup
Good for crews who talk all day

p: Add-on headsets can snag on branches or get knocked loose when you push through the canopy. An integrated arborist communication system keeps the speakers, mic and controls in place so you can focus on the work.
It makes rigging calls and drop-zone clears clear and quick, which keeps the job moving.

An integrated setup also means fewer cables and clips to snag on limbs or catch on a lanyard when you move through the crown. Controls that stay in the same place every day are easier to use with gloves on.
For crews that rely on constant communication, such as rigging-heavy removals or work near structures, it can make the whole job run smoother.
Check that the system fits your helmet model, works with your hearing protection and does not compromise the helmet's certification. Follow the helmet maker's guidance on approved accessories.
Keep hand signals and a call-and-response routine as backup, and charge the units every night.
Make sure each crew member's unit is set up and paired before the job, not in the drop zone. Do a quick radio check before the first climb, just as you would a hand-signal check.
Keep the system clean and dry as much as you can, and inspect the helmet itself as the manufacturer instructs.

faq.q: Will the Sena system fit my helmet?
faq.a: Check the listing for compatible helmets. Do not modify a helmet in ways the helmet maker does not approve.

faq.q: Can it connect to other Sena units?
faq.a: Many Sena systems connect to compatible Sena units. Check the specific model's documentation.

name: ERB Safety O.N.E. Live Free Camo Safety Glasses
title: ERB Safety O.N.E. Live Free Camo Safety Glasses
h1: ERB Safety O.N.E. Live Free Camo Safety Glasses
meta: ERB Safety O.N.E. Live Free camo safety glasses are light, low-cost eye protection for climbing, chipping and brush work. Fit, lens choice and care.
tagline: Light, low-cost camo safety glasses for everyday tree work.
summary: The ERB Safety O.N.E. Live Free glasses are camo safety glasses that give you light, comfortable eye protection for climbing, chipping and dragging brush. They are cheap enough to keep a few pairs in the truck so nobody works without them.
highlights: Camo frame with a wraparound style
Low cost, easy to stock for a crew
Works with most helmets and earmuffs
Good for chipping, brush and ground work
Check lens markings for the rating

body.h: Why eye protection matters on every job
p: Sawdust, bark flakes, twigs and chipper spit are constant on a tree job. One bad hit can take you out of work for weeks. Safety glasses are the simplest piece of protective gear there is, and they only work if they are on your face.
That is where inexpensive, comfortable glasses earn their place. If they are light and do not fog or pinch, people keep wearing them all day.

Chipper work deserves special mention. Chips and twigs kick back out of the infeed with real force, and a stray piece can hit you from an angle you do not expect. Wraparound glasses give better side coverage than flat lenses for that reason.
Grinding stumps and running a blower kick up the same kind of debris, and glasses are the minimum for both.

body.h: What the O.N.E. Live Free brings
p: ERB safety glasses are a common choice for crews that buy in bulk. The O.N.E. Live Free has a wraparound shape for side coverage and a camo frame that a lot of people simply like. It is light enough to wear under a helmet visor and slim enough to sit under earmuff cushions without breaking the seal badly.

Check the frame and lens markings for the impact rating before you rely on them for saw work, and choose a lens tint suited to the light. A dark lens is fine in full sun but a bad idea under a heavy canopy or at dusk.

Keep a box of spares in the truck. Glasses get lost, sat on and scratched, and a spare on hand means nobody has an excuse to work without them. A cord or retainer helps keep them on your neck when you push them up between cuts.

Mesh helmet visors like the Kask Zenith visor stop larger chips but let fine dust through. Many climbers wear safety glasses under a mesh visor for that reason. On the ground, around the chipper and when grinding stumps, glasses plus a face shield is the safer combination.
Follow your employer's PPE policy and the ANSI Z133 requirements for eye and face protection for the task.
If you wear prescription glasses, look at over-the-glasses safety frames or prescription safety lenses instead of trying to stack two pairs.

Rinse grit off before wiping the lens, or you will scratch it. Store them in a pouch or case rather than loose in the truck. Replace any pair with deep scratches, cracks or a loose frame. At this price there is no reason to work through a scuffed lens.
If fogging is a problem, look for an anti-fog lens or an anti-fog treatment. Glasses that fog get pushed up and left there, which defeats the purpose.

faq.q: Are ERB safety glasses ANSI rated?
faq.a: Many ERB glasses are marked for ANSI Z87.1. Check the markings on the specific frame and lens you receive.

faq.q: Can I wear camo safety glasses under a helmet visor?
faq.a: Yes. Many climbers wear safety glasses under a mesh visor to block fine dust that gets through the mesh.

faq.q: Are tinted safety glasses OK for tree work?
faq.a: In bright sun, yes. Under a dense canopy or in low light, use a clear or light lens so you can see hazards.

faq.q: How often should I replace safety glasses?
faq.a: Whenever the lens is scratched enough to affect your vision, or the frame is cracked or loose.

name: Kask Zenith Visor
title: Kask Visor: Zenith Clear Eye Visor for Kask Helmets
h1: Kask Visor for the Zenith Helmet
meta: This Kask visor for the Zenith helmet is a clear eye-protection shield that flips up when you do not need it. Fit, uses, care and typical price for climbers.
tagline: A clear flip-up eye visor for climbers wearing Kask helmets.
summary: This Kask visor is a clear eye-protection shield made for the Kask Zenith helmet and compatible Kask models, and it flips up out of the way when you do not need it. Climbers like it because it keeps eye protection on the helmet instead of in a pocket.
highlights: Always on the helmet, never lost in a pocket

p: Safety glasses get pushed up, fogged or left on the dashboard. A visor that lives on your helmet is there every time you need it, and you can flip it down in one move before starting the saw or pushing through a dense crown.
Many climbers who search for Kask visors want exactly that: eye protection that does not depend on remembering a separate pair of glasses.

A clear visor also gives some protection to the face from flying bark and twigs, which glasses alone do not. When you push through a dense crown, a flipped-down visor keeps small branches out of your eyes.

Kask makes several visors and helmets, and not every visor fits every shell. Check the listing and Kask's compatibility chart for your helmet model before ordering. If you are looking for the Kask Zenith X2 visor specifically, confirm the version matches your helmet's mount.
Make sure the visor sits clear of your nose and glasses and does not interfere with earmuffs. If you wear prescription glasses, test the fit before your first climb.
Climbers who wear glasses should check the visor does not press on the frames or fog up from breath. Mounting adjustments and the right visor version usually solve both problems.

A clear visor stops chips and twigs from reaching your eyes and gives some face coverage. Fine dust can still get around the edges, so on dusty tasks some climbers wear safety glasses underneath, such as the ERB O.N.E. Live Free.
Follow your employer's PPE policy and the ANSI Z133 requirements for eye and face protection for the task, and check the visor's markings for the rating it carries.

Mesh visors and clear visors each have a place. Mesh lets air through and does not fog, but fine dust gets through. A clear visor blocks dust better but can fog on humid days. Some climbers own both and switch with the season or the task.

Rinse dust off with water before wiping, and use a soft cloth so you do not scratch the lens. Avoid solvents and harsh cleaners that can cloud or weaken polycarbonate. Replace the visor when scratches start to affect your view or if it cracks.

Check the hinge and mounting points from time to time. A loose visor that drops unexpectedly or will not stay up is a distraction aloft. Keep a spare visor in the truck if you climb every day, since scratches build up fast in sawdust.
When the helmet goes in the truck, set it so the visor is not pressed against tools or rough surfaces.

faq.q: Does the Kask Zenith visor fit all Kask helmets?
faq.a: No. Check Kask's compatibility list for your helmet model and visor version before ordering.

faq.q: Should I wear safety glasses under a Kask visor?
faq.a: On dusty tasks, many climbers do. A visor blocks chips and debris, while glasses help keep fine dust out.

faq.q: How do I clean a Kask visor without scratching it?
faq.a: Rinse with water first, then wipe gently with a soft cloth. Avoid solvents.

faq.q: Is the Kask visor rated eye protection?
faq.a: Check the markings on the visor you receive for the standard it meets.

name: Petzl Visor for Alveo and Vertex Helmets
title: Petzl Visor for Alveo and Vertex Helmets
h1: Petzl Visor for Alveo and Vertex Helmets
meta: A clear Petzl visor for Alveo and Vertex helmets that protects your eyes from chips and debris and stows up when you do not need it. Fit and care notes.
tagline: A clear eye-protection visor made to mount on Petzl helmets.
summary: This Petzl visor is a clear eye shield made to mount on Petzl Alveo and Vertex helmets, giving climbers eye protection that stays on the helmet and flips up out of the way. It is a clean fit for crews who already wear Petzl helmets.
highlights: Stays attached, never left in the truck
specs: Petzl Alveo and Vertex helmets, check model year

p: A visor keeps your eyes covered without the hassle of glasses fogging or sliding down your nose. It flips down before a cut and back up when you need a clear view of a tie-in point or a rigging call.
Because it is part of the helmet, it is there every time, which matters more than any spec.
A clear visor also protects your face from twigs and bark when you move through a dense crown. Climbers who work in conifers or thick deciduous growth often find it more useful than glasses alone.
The visor also stays out of the way when it is flipped up, so you can read a tie-in point, check a rigging block or talk to the ground crew without taking anything off.

body.h: Fit by helmet and model year
p: Petzl has changed helmet shells and visor mounts over the years. This visor is listed for the 2018 versions of the Alveo and Vertex helmets. Check your helmet's model and year and Petzl's compatibility information before ordering, because a visor that does not lock in properly is worse than none.
Make sure the visor clears your glasses and works with your earmuffs or communication headset.
If your helmet is an older or newer model, Petzl may make a different visor for it. Ordering the right one the first time saves a return and a week of working without it.

A clear visor stops chips and twigs, but fine dust can still get around the edges, so many climbers wear safety glasses under it on dusty tasks. Follow your employer's PPE policy and ANSI Z133 for eye and face protection, and check the visor's markings for the rating it carries.
If you are building out a complete PPE kit, pair the helmet and visor with hearing protection, gloves and chainsaw safety gear for saw work.

Clear visors can fog in humid weather. If that is a problem, look at an anti-fog treatment or adjust the visor angle so air moves behind it. Mesh visors do not fog but let fine dust through, so some climbers keep both and swap depending on the job.

Rinse grit off with water before wiping, use a soft cloth, and keep solvents away from the lens. Store the helmet so the visor does not rub against tools or hardware. Replace the visor when it is scratched enough to blur your view or if it cracks.
Check the visor mounts and hinge regularly. If the visor will not stay up, drops on its own or has play in the mount, replace it. Keep a spare in the truck if you climb every day.

faq.q: Will this Petzl visor fit my helmet?
faq.a: It is listed for 2018 Alveo and Vertex helmets. Check your helmet's model and year against Petzl's compatibility chart.

faq.q: Can I wear safety glasses under the Petzl visor?
faq.a: Yes, as long as the fit is comfortable. Many climbers do on dusty tasks.

faq.q: Is the Petzl visor rated eye protection?
faq.a: Check the markings on the visor for the standard it meets.

faq.q: How do I replace a scratched visor?
faq.a: Remove the old visor following Petzl's instructions and fit the new one, making sure it locks in fully.

name: Estex Fred the Rescue Dummy
title: Fred Dummy by Estex: Aerial Rescue Training Manikin
h1: Estex Fred Dummy for Rescue Training
meta: The Estex Fred dummy is a rescue training manikin for practicing aerial rescue and casualty handling in trees without putting a real person at risk.
tagline: A rescue manikin for realistic aerial rescue training.
summary: The Estex Fred dummy is a rescue training manikin built for practicing aerial rescue and casualty handling without putting a real person at risk. Tree crews use it to rehearse getting an injured climber down, which is a skill nobody wants to learn for the first time on a real emergency.
highlights: No risk to a live volunteer
Practice casualty handling on the ground
Good for crew drills and classes
specs: Aerial rescue and casualty handling practice

body.h: Why train with a rescue dummy
p: If a climber is injured or unresponsive in a tree, the crew may have only minutes to get them down. Aerial rescue is a skill that fades without practice, and practicing on a live volunteer adds risk and never quite feels real. A dummy like Fred lets crews rehearse the whole sequence: assess, climb, take the load, and lower.
Using a heavy, limp manikin also shows you how hard it is to move a body that cannot help, which changes how crews set up their rescue systems.
Fred also works for teaching new ground workers what a rescue looks like before they ever need to support one, and for refreshing experienced climbers who have not drilled in a while.

Most companies run rescue drills at least annually, and many do them more often. Fred can be set up in a tree on a climbing system to simulate a stranded climber, then the rescuer climbs to it, transfers the load and lowers it to the ground team. On the ground, it works for practicing packaging and moving a casualty to a vehicle.

Set up drills with a qualified trainer, follow ANSI Z133 guidance on emergency response, and use the same gear your crew climbs on so the practice carries over. A pulley system like the Petzl JAG System is a common part of a rescue kit.

Rotate who plays each role in drills. The person who climbs most often may be the one who needs rescuing, so everyone on the crew, including ground workers who climb occasionally, should know how to start the emergency response and support the rescuer.

Treat the dummy as real weight. Use rated anchors and rigging, have a ground person managing the system, and never put a rescuer at risk to save a manikin. Everyone climbing during a drill uses life-support gear that meets the applicable standard, inspected before use.
Debrief after each drill. What took too long, what gear was missing, who did not know their role? Fix those before a real emergency finds them.
Time the drill from the call to the casualty reaching the ground. That number tells you more about your crew's readiness than any checklist, and it usually improves fast with practice.
Store Fred dry and out of the sun, and check seams and attachment points before each session. Wipe off mud and sap after outdoor drills so it lasts for many training days.
Keep it with the rest of your rescue kit, not buried in a shop corner. A dummy that is easy to grab gets used for drills more often.

faq.q: What is a Fred dummy used for?
faq.a: It is a rescue training manikin used to practice aerial rescue, lowering and casualty handling without a live volunteer.

faq.q: How heavy is the Fred rescue dummy?
faq.a: Check the listing for the version you order. Rescue dummies are made heavy on purpose so training feels realistic.

faq.q: How often should tree crews practice aerial rescue?
faq.a: Many companies drill at least once a year and more often for new climbers. Follow your employer's policy and ANSI Z133 guidance.

faq.q: Can Fred be used for other rescue training?
faq.a: Yes. It is useful for any training that involves moving or lowering a casualty, as long as the setup is supervised by a qualified trainer.

name: BloodStopper Gauze Kit
title: BloodStopper Gauze Kit: Blood Stopper Bandage
meta: The BloodStopper gauze kit is a blood stopper bandage and pad combo for fast pressure on cuts and wounds. Stock one in every truck and climbing kit.
tagline: A compress bandage for putting fast pressure on a bleeding wound.
summary: The BloodStopper gauze kit is a blood stopper bandage that combines a thick gauze pad with built-in wraps, so you can get pressure on a bleeding wound fast with one set of hands. It belongs in every truck first-aid kit.
highlights: Compact for truck or saddle kits
Works on arms, legs and heads

body.h: Why it belongs on the truck
p: Saw cuts, hand-saw slips and chipper injuries can bleed hard and fast. A blood stopper bandage lets one person put a thick pad on the wound and hold it with the attached wraps, which frees their hands to call for help or manage the scene.
They are cheap and small, so keep several in each truck and one in your climbing kit.
