Every crew member should know where the first-aid kit is, and it should be in the same place in every truck. When someone is bleeding, nobody should be searching through a cab.
Pair compress bandages with a tourniquet, gloves and a basic trauma kit so you can handle a range of injuries.
Check the kit after every job where it was opened, and restock right away.

A compress bandage is for bleeding that firm pressure can control. Severe limb bleeding may need a tourniquet, and any serious injury needs emergency services. Get first-aid and bleeding-control training so you know what to use when.
Check expiration and packaging regularly and restock after use.
Practice applying one in a training session so it is not the first time when it matters. Replace any bandage whose packaging is damaged or wet.

faq.q: What is a blood stopper bandage?
faq.a: It is a compress bandage with a thick gauze pad and attached tails to hold pressure on a bleeding wound.

faq.q: Can it stop severe bleeding?
faq.a: It helps with bleeding that pressure can control. For life-threatening limb bleeding, use a tourniquet and call 911.

name: Petzl JAG System
title: Petzl JAG System Haul Kit for Rescue
meta: The Petzl JAG System is a compact, ready-to-use pulley haul kit for lifting, tensioning and rescue. How crews use it, setup and typical price.
tagline: A compact, ready-to-use pulley haul kit for rescue and tensioning.
summary: The Petzl JAG System is a compact, ready-to-use pulley haul kit that gives you mechanical advantage for lifting, tensioning and rescue without building a system from scratch. Crews keep one in the rescue kit for fast setup when time counts.

body.h: Where it fits in tree work
p: In an aerial rescue, a rescuer may need to lift a casualty a short distance to release their tie-in before lowering. A pre-built haul kit like the JAG System makes that lift faster and easier than building a pulley system on the spot.
Crews also use it for tensioning lines and pulling small loads where a portable mechanical advantage helps.

Because it comes pre-rigged, there are fewer steps to remember under stress. That matters in an aerial rescue, where the rescuer may be working alone at height while the ground team manages the scene and calls for help.
A haul kit is one part of a rescue plan. Crews still need a second climbing system on site, an agreed plan for who climbs, and practice getting a casualty down.

A haul kit is only useful if you know how to rig it. Train with it before an emergency, ideally with a qualified instructor and a rescue dummy. Follow Petzl's instructions for use and rated loads. Life-support gear has to meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every use, and be used by trained climbers.
Inspect the pulleys, rope and connectors before each use and retire anything damaged.
Store it in a dedicated, labeled bag with the rest of your rescue gear so it is not borrowed for routine rigging and left damaged.

faq.q: What is the Petzl JAG System used for?
faq.a: It is a compact pulley haul kit for lifting, tensioning and rescue, ready to clip in and use.

faq.q: Do I need training to use the JAG System?
faq.a: Yes. Rescue hauling is a skill. Train with it under a qualified instructor before relying on it.

name: WoundSeal Stop Bleeding Powder
title: WoundSeal Powder for Stopping Bleeding
meta: WoundSeal is a powder for stopping bleeding from minor cuts and scrapes. It forms a quick seal over the wound. When to use it and when to call for help.
tagline: A powder that seals minor cuts and nicks fast on the job.
summary: WoundSeal is a powder for stopping bleeding from minor cuts, scrapes and nicks by forming a protective seal over the wound. It is a handy addition to a truck first-aid kit for the small cuts that come with handling saws, files and brush.
highlights: Compact for truck and saddle kits
Handy for nicks from chain and files
Easy to apply with one hand

p: Filing chain, changing bars and dragging brush lead to a steady stream of small cuts that keep bleeding into your gloves. A powder that stops bleeding on contact lets you seal a nick and get back to work.
Read the package directions and warnings before you need it, so you know how to apply it correctly.
Small cuts matter on a tree job because they get dirty fast and a bleeding hand makes it hard to grip a saw or a rope safely. Sealing the cut lets you clean up, cover it and keep working safely.
Keep a pack in the truck kit and one in your saddle pocket or climbing bag for small injuries aloft.

Powder for minor bleeding is not a substitute for direct pressure, a compress bandage or a tourniquet on a serious wound. Deep cuts, saw injuries and heavy bleeding need firm pressure and emergency services right away.
Get first-aid and bleeding-control training so your crew knows when to use each item in the kit.
Check the expiration date on your kit and replace it after use. Keep a separate supply of gloves and bandages so you can clean and cover the wound once the bleeding stops.

faq.q: What powder stops bleeding?
faq.a: Products like WoundSeal use a powder that forms a seal over minor wounds. Follow the label and use it only for the injuries it is meant for.

faq.q: Can I use WoundSeal on a chainsaw cut?
faq.a: Not as the main treatment. Serious saw cuts need direct pressure, possibly a tourniquet, and emergency care.

name: Husqvarna Technical Gloves
title: Husqvarna Chainsaw Gloves: Technical Work Gloves
meta: Husqvarna chainsaw gloves from the Technical line give grip and dexterity for running a saw, felling and bucking. Fit, saw protection and care notes.
tagline: Dexterous work gloves for saw work, felling and bucking.
summary: The Technical line of Husqvarna chainsaw gloves is built for people who run a saw all day and still want enough feel to work the controls, file chain and handle wedges. They sit in a good middle ground between thin climbing gloves and heavy rigging gloves.
highlights: Built for saw work and handling
Good dexterity for controls and filing
Reinforced palm for grip and wear
Check the label for saw protection
specs: Varies by version; check the label

p: If you are on the ground felling, bucking and limbing most of the day, you want gloves that grip the saw handles firmly, take vibration and still let you feel the throttle and chain brake. Husqvarna gloves in the Technical line are made for exactly that kind of work.
They are also handy for climbers who run a top-handle saw and want more protection than a thin climbing glove without losing too much feel.
Ground crews also like them for handling wedges, felling levers and log tongs, where a solid grip and a reinforced palm make a difference over a full day of bucking.

Some Husqvarna chainsaw gloves include cut-protective material on the back of the left hand, which is the hand most exposed to the chain if you get a kickback. Others are general work gloves. Check the label of the exact version you buy to see whether it has saw protection and what standard it meets.
Either way, gloves are the last line of defense. A sharp chain, a working chain brake, proper body position and good technique matter more.

Remember that most chainsaw injuries to the hands come from kickback and from touching the chain while the engine is idling or coasting. Keep the chain brake engaged when walking with the saw, and never reach for the bar or chain with the engine running, gloves or not.

A glove that is too big lets your hand slide around and reduces control; one that is too tight tires your hands and wears fast. Measure around your palm and check Husqvarna's size chart. Try them on with the saw you use most, especially if you run a top-handle saw aloft.
Keep a spare pair in the truck. Wet gloves are cold, slippery and wear out faster.
Vibration is part of saw work, and gloves that fit well help you hold the saw with a relaxed grip instead of a death grip, which is easier on your hands over a long season.

Knock off sawdust and let them air dry away from direct heat, which can stiffen leather and synthetic palms. Retire them when the palm wears through, seams open or any cut-protective layer is damaged. Pair them with chainsaw protective pants or chaps and the rest of your PPE every time you run a saw.
If you climb in them, check that the gloves do not catch in your hitch or hardware. Some climbers keep a thinner pair for climbing and switch to the Technical gloves for saw work on the ground.

faq.q: Are Husqvarna Technical gloves chainsaw protective?
faq.a: It depends on the version. Some include saw protection on the left hand; others are general work gloves. Check the label.

faq.q: What size Husqvarna gloves should I buy?
faq.a: Measure around your palm and use Husqvarna's size chart. Aim for a snug fit without pinching.

faq.q: Can I climb in Husqvarna Technical gloves?
faq.a: Many climbers do, especially when running a saw aloft. Make sure you still have good feel for your hitch and hardware.

faq.q: How do I dry wet work gloves?
faq.a: Air dry them away from direct heat. High heat can stiffen and crack the palms.

name: Wonder Grip Gloves
title: Wonder Grip Gloves for Climbing and Ground Work
meta: Wonder Grip gloves are thin, coated work gloves with strong grip and good feel for climbing, rigging and handling hardware. Fit, uses and care.
tagline: Thin, grippy coated gloves that let you feel your hitch and hardware.
summary: Wonder Grip gloves are thin, coated work gloves that give strong grip and close fit, so climbers can feel their hitch, clip carabiners and tie knots without taking them off. They are cheap enough to buy by the dozen and swap out as they wear.
highlights: Lets you feel hitches and hardware
Inexpensive enough to buy in bulk
Good for climbing, rigging and ground work

body.h: Why climbers like thin coated gloves
p: Climbing calls for a lot of fine work: tending a hitch, tying knots, opening gates and threading a throw line. Heavy gloves make that clumsy. Wonder gloves have a thin knit liner and a grippy coating on the palm and fingers, so you keep most of your feel and still protect your hands from bark and rope.
They are also popular with ground crews for rigging, handling brush and loading the chipper, where grip on rope and wet wood matters.

Wonder Grip gloves come in several versions with different coatings and liners. A basic nitrile-style coating suits most dry work, while some versions are designed for better grip in wet or oily conditions. Check the listing to choose the one that fits your work.

Thin coated gloves are not cut-resistant and offer no saw protection. For running a saw on the ground, use gloves suited to that task, such as Husqvarna Technical gloves. For heavy rigging with fast-running rope, a thicker glove can save your palms from friction burns.
Coatings also wear through faster than leather. That is the trade for dexterity, and at this price most crews just treat them as consumables.
They are also not insulated, so on cold mornings some climbers wear a thin liner underneath or switch to a warmer glove until things heat up.
Around the chipper, avoid any glove with loose cuffs or worn, ragged fingers that could catch on brush being pulled into the infeed. A snug glove in good condition is safer than a worn one.

A snug fit is the whole point. Too loose and the fingertips bunch up when you tie knots. Too tight and they tear at the seams. Check the size chart and keep a couple of sizes on hand if you buy for a crew.
Some versions are sold with longer cuffs or different coatings. Pick the coating that suits your conditions, and keep spares in the truck for wet days.
If you climb most days, many climbers find two pairs per day works well: one for the morning and a dry pair for the afternoon. Grip is noticeably better when the gloves are dry.
Rinse off sap and dirt, and let them air dry. Throw them out when the coating wears through at the fingertips or the seams split, because worn coatings lose grip quickly.
Keep a stack in the truck. Fresh gloves are cheap, and climbing in worn-out ones that have lost their grip is not worth it.

faq.q: Are Wonder Grip gloves good for climbing?
faq.a: Many climbers like them for dexterity and grip on rope and hardware. They do not offer cut protection, so they are not for saw work on the ground.

faq.q: What is the difference between Wonder gloves and leather work gloves?
faq.a: Wonder gloves are thinner and give more feel, while leather lasts longer and protects better against friction and abrasion.

faq.q: How long do Wonder Grip gloves last?
faq.a: It depends on use. Daily climbers may go through a pair in a week or two. They are inexpensive, so most crews buy them in bulk.

faq.q: Can I wash Wonder Grip gloves?
faq.a: Rinse them and let them air dry. Avoid high heat, which can damage the coating.
